items.name: Recovery test — recover into us-east-2 (Phase 1, no promotion)
preconditions: THIS RUNBOOK DOES NOT MOVE PRODUCTION. The adjudication Aurora global cluster keeps its writer in us-east-1 for the whole window. The drill writes to a restored copy (stp_a06b), never to the claims ledger. If what you actually need is a promotion, you are looking at a Phase 2 game day: use the game-day wrapper with the region-switch runbook, which fences the old primary BEFORE any promotion and carries the Branch A/B rollback. Do not improvise a promotion out of this runbook.
Phase 0 checklist green and signed off
Every Tier-0 store has a current replication path, checked in the week before the window and re-checked at T0 (stp_a01)
Operator and approver both on the calendar for the full window
Rollback owner named, and able to recite stp_r00 (establish who holds the writer; return it if it moved) from memory before the window opens
A recent adjudication cluster snapshot exists to build the drill copy from — you must supply its identifier in stp_a06b; without it there is nothing for the success bar to write to
T0 definition agreed: T0 = the first recovery action is executed (the recovery-region apply)

steps.title: Pre-flight: record T0, record who holds the writer, and prove every replication path is current
steps.detail: Open the test record and write wall-clock T0 the moment the first recovery action runs. Record which region holds the adjudication writer RIGHT NOW, before anything else happens — it should be us-east-1, and stp_r00 compares against this line at the end. Then read each mechanism's own freshness signal, because current lag IS your RPA if the event is now: Aurora Global Database replica lag (adjudication), the age of the newest AWS Backup copy (pricing), ReplicationStatus on recently written objects (S3 CRR), replication state on the newest image tags (ECR), replica presence for every secret on the signed-off list, and — for the two components still on point-in-time recovery, the remittance cluster and the claim queues — recovery points from the same aligned sync. Screenshot the lot: this is the RPA evidence.
steps.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --region us-east-2 --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[?IsWriter].DBClusterArn" --output text
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag --dimensions Name=DBClusterIdentifier,Value=<us-east-2-secondary-cluster-id> --start-time <T0-15min> --end-time <T0> --period 60 --statistics Maximum --region us-east-2
aws s3api head-object --bucket <claims-bucket> --key <object-written-this-morning> --region us-east-1 --query ReplicationStatus
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name adjudication --region us-east-2 --query "imageDetails[0].imagePushedAt"
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --region us-east-2 --query "length(SecretList)"
aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name acme-dr --region us-east-2 --max-results 5 --query "RecoveryPoints[0].CompletionDate"
arpio recovery-points list --environment <env>   # the two point-in-time stores: confirm both points come from the SAME sync
# You must supply: the bucket and a recently written key, the secondary cluster id, and the vendor environment name.
steps.verify: Writer member is the us-east-1 cluster ARN (recorded verbatim); global-cluster lag under a minute; CRR ReplicationStatus COMPLETED on recent objects; ECR tags present in us-east-2; replica secrets present; the two point-in-time stores showing aligned recovery points none older than 30 min
steps.pass: Every in-scope store has a recorded, current position, and the writer ARN at T0 is written down; screenshots in the record
steps.record: T0; the adjudication writer ARN at T0; per-store lag or recovery-point age

steps.title: Pre-flight: DECIDE containment — the runtime proof is stp_a05b, not this step
steps.detail:
Containment stays ON for tests — it is what stops a drill POSTing a real claim to the clearinghouse, uploading a real settlement file, or firing a real webhook (dec_sandbox_v2). This step used to ask the operator to run `describe-vpc-endpoints` against `<recovery-vpc>` — a VPC that stp_a04 has not built yet. A gate nobody can execute is a gate everybody waves through, so the check has been split in two and this half only asks for what is knowable before anything is launched.

CHECKABLE NOW: (1) the third-party tool's network sandbox flag for the resources IT recovers; (2) the recovery-region IaC — containment is a property of the code before it is a property of a VPC, so read the module: no 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway or internet gateway, and the endpoint list complete (ecr.api, ecr.dkr, the S3 GATEWAY endpoint — ECR layers live in S3 and without it pulls fail after the manifest and look like a mystery network fault — plus secretsmanager, sts, kms, logs); (3) if containment is being relaxed, the named approver and the acknowledgement recorded verbatim.

NOT CHECKABLE NOW, and this step must not pretend otherwise: whether the running environment can actually reach a partner. That is stp_a05b, run from inside the recovered environment once the platform exists, and it is the one with teeth.
steps.command:
arpio environment show <env> --settings   # expect network sandbox / isolated networking = ON for the resources it recovers
grep -rn "aws_nat_gateway\|aws_internet_gateway\|0.0.0.0/0" envs/dr-us-east-2/ || echo "no default route to the internet in the recovery VPC module"
terragrunt run-all plan --terragrunt-working-dir envs/dr-us-east-2 | grep -E "vpc_endpoint|nat_gateway|internet_gateway"
steps.verify: Vendor sandbox ON for the resources it recovers; the recovery-region module creates all seven VPC endpoints and adds no 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT or internet gateway; if containment is being relaxed, the verbatim acknowledgement and the approver's name are already in the record
steps.pass: Containment DESIGN proven in the tool's settings and in the code, and the decision recorded with a name against it. This step does not prove containment at runtime and does not claim to — stp_a05b does that, and it is allowed to stop the test.
steps.record: Sandbox flag as launched; endpoint list from the plan; any relax decision and its approver

steps.title: Prove the image path before anything needs it
steps.detail: ECR replication runs continuously, so the images should already be in us-east-2 — "should" is the word this step exists to remove. Confirm all 17 repositories and the expected tags are present, then prove a real pull from inside the recovery VPC over the endpoints. Images pushed before the replication rule was created were never replicated, and repository settings and lifecycle policies do not replicate at all (repository creation templates are the supported way to carry those across).
steps.command: aws ecr describe-repositories --region us-east-2 --query "length(repositories)" && aws ecr describe-images --repository-name adjudication --region us-east-2 --query "imageDetails[0].imageTags"
steps.verify: All 17 repositories present with the tags the deployments reference, and a test pull succeeds from the recovery VPC
steps.pass: Repositories and tags present; pull succeeds without internet egress
steps.record: Repository/tag count; any tag missing in the recovery region

steps.title: Build the recovery-region estate
steps.detail: Apply the recovery-region IaC — VPC, EKS and node pools, queues, API Gateway and VPC Link — and start the point-in-time recovery of the two components that are not continuously replicated (the remittance cluster and the claim queues). The adjudication database endpoint is an INPUT to this apply: leave it unset here and set it to the drill cluster in stp_a06b. Do NOT promote or fail over the Aurora global cluster — not at this step and not at any step in this runbook; the writer stays in us-east-1 (stp_a06 says why). Cold-start duration from here is the number leadership asks about — last measured ~40 min.
steps.verify: Apply completes with no failed resources; the point-in-time restores report done; no resource in the plan touches the acme-adjudication-global cluster or its us-east-1 members
steps.pass: Estate built, zero failed resources, and nothing in the apply changed the production global cluster
steps.record: Apply start/finish; failed or skipped resources

steps.title: Verify platform: nodes, mesh, DNS, controllers
steps.detail: Nodes Ready, CoreDNS resolving, istiod up, ALB controller and Karpenter running. Do not look at app pods yet — a broken platform makes every app failure a red herring. Pass --context on every kubectl in this runbook: whatever the kubeconfig last pointed at is not an argument you want to have with yourself at 3am.
steps.command: kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get nodes && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get pods -n kube-system && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get pods -n istio-system
steps.verify: All nodes Ready; CoreDNS/istiod/ALB controller/Karpenter Running; the context name in the prompt is the recovery cluster

steps.title: Containment probe: prove from INSIDE the recovered environment that no partner endpoint is reachable
steps.detail:
This is the half of stp_a02 that needed a cluster to exist. Run it now: the platform is up, so there is somewhere to run it, and the app workloads have not yet been given any work to do. A recovered environment is a faithful copy of production — same credentials, same config, same endpoints — so with an open egress path it will do production things.

Run the probe from a pod on the recovery cluster, in the tier-0 namespace, on the same subnet and security group the workloads will use. If the image has neither curl nor nc the probe proves nothing: rerun it in one that does, rather than recording a row of silence as a pass.

If anything comes back REACHABLE: do not start app workloads. Fix the route or the security group, or stop the test. "We will be careful" is not a control, and the thing being prevented — a drill claim arriving at the clearinghouse — cannot be un-sent.
steps.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run dr-containment-probe --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/<image-with-curl-or-nc>:<tag> -- sh -c 'for ep in <clearinghouse-host> <settlement-sftp-host> <payment-provider-host> <prod-db-host>; do if curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "https://$ep"; then echo "REACHABLE: $ep"; elif command -v nc >/dev/null && nc -z -w 5 "$ep" 443; then echo "REACHABLE: $ep"; else echo "blocked: $ep"; fi; done'
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get cronjobs -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SUSPEND:.spec.suspend
aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --region us-east-2 --query "EventSourceMappings[?State=='Enabled'].[UUID,FunctionArn]" --output table
steps.verify: Zero "REACHABLE:" lines across every partner and production endpoint on the list, and the probe demonstrably ran (at least one "blocked:" line per endpoint, from a tool that exists in the image); every outbound cronjob SUSPEND=true; no enabled event-source mapping in us-east-2 that would start pulling real work
steps.pass: Containment proven from inside the recovered environment, not asserted. Any REACHABLE line = stop here and do not start app workloads; if containment was deliberately relaxed, the approver's verbatim acknowledgement from stp_a02 must already be in the record and the reachable endpoint must be one the approval names.
steps.record: Endpoints tested and the probe output verbatim; cronjob suspend states; event-source-mapping list

steps.title: Adjudication data: measure the RPA from replica lag — this runbook does NOT promote the production writer
steps.detail:
The adjudication cluster is an Aurora Global Database whose writer is production, live, and in us-east-1. This runbook never moves it. Read that twice, because the August run did move it, and that is why this step was rewritten (dec_nopromote).

WHY NOT, in order of what it costs you:
1. This is Phase 1: DNS is untouched and every us-east-1 pod keeps serving. Moving the writer to us-east-2 while the front door still points at us-east-1 does not test an outage, it causes one — live writes start failing the instant the promotion completes. The test becomes the incident.
2. An Aurora global FAILOVER is the lossy operation. It loses whatever had not shipped, and it does not demote the old writer for you, so both regions can accept writes. Two writers on a claims ledger is the one failure worse than downtime, and this runbook has no fence step because it has nothing to fence — it does not promote.
3. A planned SWITCHOVER is the lossless one (Aurora syncs the secondary first, so RPO 0, and it demotes the old writer) — but it still needs a healthy primary, a quiesced old region and a real approval, and it still moves production. That is a Phase 2 game day, not a drill.
4. You do not need any of it for the number. The adjudication RPA is the replica lag at T0. A promotion would measure how long a promotion takes, which is an RTA input, not an RPA.

WHAT THIS STEP DOES: record AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag at T0, prove the us-east-2 secondary is a real, current, queryable copy by reading it through its READER endpoint, and then prove the writer has not moved. If it has moved, the test stops and you go to stp_r00 before anything is destroyed.
steps.command:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag --dimensions Name=DBClusterIdentifier,Value=<us-east-2-secondary-cluster-id> --start-time <T0> --end-time <T0+5min> --period 60 --statistics Maximum --region us-east-2
# Run this one from a pod INSIDE the recovery VPC — the secondary is not reachable from your laptop:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run dr-freshness --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/psql:<tag> -- psql -h <adjudication-secondary-READER-endpoint> -c "SELECT max(created_at) AS newest_row FROM claims"
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --region us-east-2 --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[?IsWriter].DBClusterArn" --output text
steps.verify: Lag recorded in seconds with its timestamp; the secondary answers the read-only query and newest_row is within the measured lag of T0; the writer member ARN is still arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster:acme-adjudication-aurora
steps.pass: Adjudication RPA written down as a lag measured at T0, AND the writer is provably still in us-east-1. A writer ARN in us-east-2 means production moved: stop the test and run stp_r00 before anything else.
steps.record: AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag at T0 (seconds); newest_row timestamp from the reader endpoint; the writer ARN returned by the no-promotion check

steps.title: Give the drill a WRITABLE adjudication copy — restore a drill cluster, never the production writer
steps.detail:
The success bar writes: adjudicating a test claim inserts rows. Those rows land in a copy, not in the claims ledger. Restore a separate, obviously-named cluster in us-east-2 from a cross-region snapshot copy — acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> — and point the recovered deployments at IT.

Two ways this goes wrong, both seen in the wild:
(a) the pods are pointed at the global cluster's us-east-2 READER endpoint, where every write dies with "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction" and an hour disappears into debugging the application;
(b) the pods are pointed at the us-east-1 writer, in which case the drill is quietly writing test claims into production and the L6 bar passes for entirely the wrong reason. This one does not announce itself. Check the DSN; do not assume it.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE, and the record must say so: it does not measure how long a promotion takes and it does not prove the promotion works. A drill copy proves the data is there and the application can run on it. The drill cluster's own freshness is the age of the snapshot it came from — that is NOT the adjudication RPA, which is the lag from stp_a06. Do not let the two numbers get confused in the test record; they measure different things and the snapshot age is always the worse of the two.
steps.command:
aws rds copy-db-cluster-snapshot --source-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier <arn-of-recent-us-east-1-snapshot> --target-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> --kms-key-id <us-east-2-cmk> --source-region us-east-1 --region us-east-2
aws rds restore-db-cluster-from-snapshot --db-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> --snapshot-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> --engine aurora-postgresql --db-subnet-group-name <recovery-db-subnet-group> --vpc-security-group-ids <recovery-db-sg> --region us-east-2   # without the subnet group and SG it lands somewhere nothing can reach
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD>-1 --db-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> --db-instance-class <class-matching-production-load> --engine aurora-postgresql --region us-east-2
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run dr-drill-write --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/psql:<tag> -- psql -h <drill-writer-endpoint> -c "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dr_drill_marker(t timestamptz); INSERT INTO dr_drill_marker VALUES (now()); SELECT count(*) FROM dr_drill_marker;"
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get deploy -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}/{.metadata.name}={.spec.template.spec.containers[*].env[?(@.name=="DB_HOST")].value}{"\n"}{end}'
steps.verify: Drill cluster Status available under an identifier containing "drill"; the marker INSERT succeeds, so it is genuinely writable; every DB_HOST in the recovered namespaces resolves to the drill endpoint — zero pointing at the global cluster's reader endpoint and zero pointing at any us-east-1 host
steps.pass: The apps will write to a copy, evidenced by one successful write to the drill cluster plus a DSN listing containing no us-east-1 host and no global-cluster endpoint. If you cannot produce that listing, do not start the app workloads.
steps.record: Drill cluster id; the source snapshot id and its creation time (the drill copy's own age — NOT the adjudication RPA); the DSN listing

steps.title: Every other store: freshness at T0, and whether the recovery points were aligned
steps.detail:
One RPA number per store, each with its mechanism next to it, each derived from T0. The remittance cluster came back from a point-in-time recovery point rather than continuous replication: record the newest row as a TIMESTAMP and subtract T0 yourself. Do not use `now() - max(settled_at)` — on a restored database that takes no writes during the test, that measures the RPA plus however long the test has been running, and it is how a 30-minute configuration reports as two hours. Test #2's 118 minutes was measured that way and should be treated as an upper bound until it is re-measured against T0 (gap_rpa1).

Alignment is the other half. The object, queue and database recovery points must come from the same sync set; in test #2 they did not, and nobody checked because nobody had been asked to. Two stores whose recovery points are minutes apart give you a state your application has never seen.

The queues are the clearest shape-versus-bytes case in this workspace: what comes back is the QUEUE and its configuration. No tool, vendor or AWS-native, moves SQS messages across regions. In-flight loss is accepted and documented (dec_mechanisms) — it is not something to discover here.
steps.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n remittance run dr-freshness-rem --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/psql:<tag> -- psql -h <recovered-remittance-endpoint> -c "SELECT max(settled_at) AS newest_row FROM remittances"   # from inside the recovery VPC. RPA(remittance) = T0 - newest_row; record BOTH timestamps, not just the difference
aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name acme-dr --region us-east-2 --query "RecoveryPoints[?contains(ResourceArn,'pricing')].[CompletionDate,Status]" --output table   # the copy's age is the pricing RPA, and 24 h is the decision, not an oversight
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier <recovered-pricing-cluster> --region us-east-2 --query "DBClusters[0].Status"
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url <recovered-claim-queue-url> --attribute-names All --region us-east-2
steps.verify: newest_row recorded as a timestamp beside T0 for the remittance cluster; the pricing cluster available from a copy no older than 24 h (its RPO by decision, not an oversight); both queues present with the expected redrive policy and visibility timeout; the recovery points used for database, objects and queues all named, with their sync ids
steps.pass: An RPA number written down for EVERY store, not just the fast one, each subtracted from T0 rather than from now(). Any two stores whose recovery points are not from the same sync set is a finding on the spot (gap_rpa1).
steps.record: Per store: mechanism, newest-row or recovery-point timestamp, T0, and the subtraction; sync ids for the point-in-time stores

steps.title: Verify secrets: the app’s own identity can decrypt them (tests die HERE)
steps.detail: `describe-secret` proves only that a secret exists — not its value, not that KMS will decrypt it, and not that the workload’s identity may read it. Prove the real thing: run `get-secret-value` (which forces kms:Decrypt) AS THE WORKLOAD’S OWN IDENTITY, with `sts get-caller-identity` beside it so the evidence shows the app role and not an admin. Best: exec into the real workload. Next best: a probe pod bound to the same ServiceAccount. Otherwise: the app’s own secrets-init probe passing — and if you fall back to reading its logs, capture them first and assert the capture is non-empty, because a `kubectl logs` that failed pipes nothing into grep and an empty grep looks exactly like a clean run.
steps.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> exec -n <tier0-ns> deploy/<workload> -- sh -c 'aws sts get-caller-identity; aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <name> --region us-east-2 --query SecretString --output text >/dev/null && echo DECRYPT_OK'
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --region us-east-2 --query "SecretList[].Name" --output text | tr "\t" "\n" | sort > present.txt && sort signed-off-secrets.txt > needed.txt && comm -23 needed.txt present.txt   # ANY output = MISSING
steps.verify: Caller identity IS the application role (not the node instance role, not an admin), every runtime secret returns DECRYPT_OK, and the reconciliation diff against the signed-off list is empty
steps.pass: DECRYPT_OK for every secret the workload mounts, proven under the app role, and nothing on the signed-off list missing in us-east-2. Anything else is a blocker finding — stop here rather than starting apps and debugging L4 symptoms of an L3 cause.
steps.record: Caller identity returned; missing secrets → immediate blocker finding; the diff output verbatim

steps.title: Verify applications: pods up, images from us-east-2 registry, writing to the drill copy
steps.detail: Confirm adjudication, remittance, pharmacy and pricing are all Ready after the GitOps sync — and that every image reference points at the us-east-2 registry. A pod pulling cross-region from us-east-1 passes the test and fails the disaster. Sweep initContainers as well as containers: secrets-init is an initContainer, and it is the container stp_a07 is about, so an image sweep that reads containers[0] misses the one that matters most. Re-confirm here that the adjudication DSN is still the drill endpoint from stp_a06b — a GitOps sync can put the production value back underneath you.
steps.command: kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get deploy -A && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{range .spec.initContainers[*]}{.image}{"\n"}{end}{range .spec.containers[*]}{.image}{"\n"}{end}{end}' | sort -u
steps.verify: Tier-0/1 deployments Ready; zero images referencing us-east-1, across initContainers and containers alike; adjudication DSN still points at the drill cluster
steps.pass: Apps Ready on recovery-region images, writing to the drill copy
steps.record: Launch-to-Ready duration (cold start); any image or DSN still pointing at us-east-1

steps.title: Verify edge WITHOUT touching DNS
steps.detail: Hit the recovered API Gateway execute-api endpoint directly with a Host header for the real domain. Public DNS is never changed in Phase 1. Certificates are regional: -k is kept because the SNI name will legitimately mismatch when you spoof the Host header, so prove the recovery-region certificate separately rather than letting -k hide its absence until game day.
steps.command:
curl -sk https://<recovery-execute-api>.execute-api.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/api/switch/healthcheck -H 'Host: api.acme-pharmacy.example'
openssl s_client -connect <recovery-edge-host>:443 -servername api.acme-pharmacy.example </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -ext subjectAltName
steps.verify: HTTP 200 through API GW → VPC Link → NLB → recovered pods; a valid us-east-2 certificate covering api.acme-pharmacy.example, unexpired
steps.pass: Healthcheck 200 with backend IPs listed, and a recovery-region certificate that would actually serve the real hostname
steps.record: Endpoint + response snippet; certificate SANs and expiry

steps.title: Success bar 1: test claim answered end-to-end
steps.detail: Submit the partner-shaped test claim against the direct endpoint. A real adjudication response with a claim_id — not a 500 — is what 'recovered' means. First success = T1. Then confirm the row landed in the DRILL cluster: a claim_id in the response proves the application answered, and the row in the drill database proves it answered from the recovered data path and not from somewhere it should not have been writing.
steps.command:
curl -sk -X POST https://<recovery-endpoint>/ncpdp -H 'Host: api.acme-pharmacy.example' -d @test-claim.json
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run dr-claim-check --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/psql:<tag> -- psql -h <drill-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT claim_id, created_at FROM claims ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1"   # from inside the recovery VPC, as in stp_a06
steps.verify: Business response with claim_id, and that same claim_id is the newest row in the drill cluster
steps.pass: Claim adjudicated end-to-end against the recovered stack; the row is in the drill copy and not in production; T1 recorded; RTA = T1 − T0
steps.record: T1; computed RTA; the claim_id and which cluster it landed in

steps.title: Success bar 2: settlement path runs
steps.detail: Kick the remittance import against the recovered bucket/queue and confirm rows land in the recovered remittance Aurora. Front-door success with a dead settlement path is still an outage for finance. Pass --context: this is a job that writes, and the cluster it writes to should never be decided by whatever the kubeconfig last pointed at.
steps.command: kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n remittance create job --from=cronjob/era-import dr-test-import && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n remittance logs -f job/dr-test-import
steps.verify: Import completes; rows in recovered remittance DB
steps.pass: Settlement path clean end-to-end, against the recovered remittance cluster

steps.title: Conclude: no teardown without explicit approval, and no teardown before the writer check
steps.detail: Teardown only on the approver's written go, and only after stp_r00 has answered the one question that decides whether teardown is safe: which region holds the adjudication writer. Concluding the vendor recovery destroys the restored copies, which is intended and irreversible. Failback is not a test action at all: if the writer moved during this window, returning it is a real switchover of a real production cluster and it belongs to stp_r00 with its own gate, not to a reflex at the end of a long day (dec_nofailback).
steps.command: # No command, and deliberately so: this is a human decision. You must supply the approver's own words — paste the approval message, with its timestamp and the approver's name, into the test record, and paste the writer ARN that stp_r00 returned next to it.
steps.verify: Written approval from the named approver in the channel, and stp_r00's writer check recorded
steps.pass: Approval captured and the writer's location known before any teardown begins
steps.record: Approver, timestamp, writer ARN at approval time

steps.title: Triage findings same-day: gaps, tickets, runbook edits
steps.detail: Write the record while it hurts. Every surprise becomes a gap with severity, a ticket, or an edit to this runbook — usually all three. Include what the test could NOT prove as well as what it did: a partner path that containment kept you from exercising is still an open risk after a green run, and a reader who only sees the passes will think otherwise.
steps.command: # No command: you must supply the findings. One line per surprise, each ending in a gap id or a ticket id, plus a short list of what this run could NOT prove (today: the partner path, and the public-DNS step that Phase 1 never performs). A finding with no destination is a finding you will rediscover during the event.
steps.verify: Every finding has a gap id or ticket next to it, and the record names what the test did not cover
steps.pass: Record written same day; findings filed; unproven paths listed explicitly
steps.record: Findings with severities and destinations; the list of things this run could not prove

rollback.title: FIRST: establish which region holds the adjudication writer, and return the writer if it moved
rollback.detail:
Nothing is destroyed until this question has an answer in the record. If you cannot tell, assume it moved and go and check — `terragrunt destroy` run while us-east-2 holds the writer is not a rollback, it is a second and larger outage, self-inflicted, on the claims ledger.

This runbook does not promote (stp_a06), so the expected answer is "us-east-1, nothing to return" and this step costs two minutes. It exists for the cases where the answer is different: someone ran a game-day path out of this window, an unplanned failover fired during the test, or the old August habit came back.

IF THE WRITER IS IN us-east-2, the return is a SWITCHOVER, not a failover, and the order is the whole point:
1. Quiesce us-east-2 first — scale the recovered deployments to zero and suspend the cronjobs — so nothing is in flight across the cut. A switchover taken with traffic still flowing is where you lose the transactions nobody expected to lose.
2. Confirm application connections to the us-east-2 writer are zero. Scope the count to your application database, application user and client backends: rdsadmin sessions, replication senders and background workers are always there, and a bare count will never reach zero.
3. `aws rds switchover-global-cluster` — graceful. Aurora syncs the secondary before it changes anything, so RPO is 0, and it demotes the old writer for you. That is exactly why you do not reach for failover on the way back.
4. VERIFY, three ways: the writer member ARN is the us-east-1 cluster; a real write succeeds against the us-east-1 writer endpoint; us-east-2 is reporting as a secondary with replication lag again.
5. Only then bring us-east-1's workloads back and let it settle.

Failing back is a SECOND switchover with the same risks. If us-east-1 is not healthy, do NOT switch back on the day: record the state, hold the quiesce, and schedule it with the approver.

NOT SAFELY REVERSIBLE: any write accepted in us-east-2 while it held the writer. A switchover returns the writer; it does not reconcile those rows. Name the reconciliation owner in this record before you cut, not after.
rollback.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --region us-east-2 --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[?IsWriter].DBClusterArn" --output text
# If that is the us-east-1 ARN: nothing to return. Record it, then go to stp_r01.
# If it is the us-east-2 ARN, in this order and no other:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> scale deploy --all --replicas=0
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get cronjobs -A -o custom-columns=:.metadata.namespace,:.metadata.name --no-headers | while read ns n; do kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n "$ns" patch cronjob "$n" -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'; done   # -o name drops the namespace and would patch whatever namespace you happen to be in
psql -h <us-east-2-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname='adjudication' AND usename='adjudication_app' AND backend_type='client backend'"
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster:acme-adjudication-aurora --region us-east-2
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --region us-east-1 --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[?IsWriter].DBClusterArn" --output text
psql -h <us-east-1-writer-endpoint> -c "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dr_return_marker(t timestamptz); INSERT INTO dr_return_marker VALUES (now());"
rollback.verify: Writer member ARN is arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster:acme-adjudication-aurora; the INSERT against the us-east-1 writer endpoint succeeds; us-east-2 reports as a secondary with replication lag again; and, if a switchover was performed, the client-backend connection count to us-east-2 was zero BEFORE it was issued
rollback.pass: Either the writer never left and the us-east-1 ARN is recorded with a timestamp, or the writer has been returned and a real write proves it. Nothing is destroyed until one of those two lines is in the record.
rollback.record: Writer ARN before and after; connection count at the cut; switchover start/finish; the verifying write; and, if the writer had moved, the named owner for reconciling writes taken in us-east-2

rollback.title: Tear down the drill estate — in order, and only after stp_r00
rollback.detail:
Order matters on the way down as much as on the way up.
1. Stop the things that write: scale the recovered deployments to zero and confirm the cronjobs are suspended.
2. Decide in writing what happens to the drill cluster's data. If anything in it is evidence, take a final snapshot; otherwise delete with --skip-final-snapshot and say that you chose to.
3. Delete the DRILL cluster explicitly, by name, after listing the clusters whose identifier contains "drill". This is the command in the whole runbook most likely to hit the wrong thing; read the name back before you run it.
4. Then destroy the IaC estate.
5. Then conclude the vendor recovery for the two point-in-time components. Concluding destroys the restored copies — that is the intent, and it is irreversible, so export anything anyone still needs out of the restored remittance cluster before this line, not after it.

`destroy` is not a rollback and never was: it is the last step of one. It is safe here only because stp_r00 proved the writer is in us-east-1 and step 1 above proved nothing in us-east-2 is still being written to.
rollback.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> scale deploy --all --replicas=0
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get cronjobs -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,SUSPEND:.spec.suspend   # every one must read true before anything is deleted
aws rds describe-db-clusters --region us-east-2 --query "DBClusters[?contains(DBClusterIdentifier,'drill')].DBClusterIdentifier" --output text
aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD>-1 --skip-final-snapshot --region us-east-2   # instances first: a cluster with members will refuse to delete
aws rds delete-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-drill-<YYYYMMDD> --skip-final-snapshot --region us-east-2
terragrunt run-all destroy --terragrunt-working-dir envs/dr-us-east-2
arpio recover conclude --environment <app-env>
rollback.verify: The only clusters deleted are the ones whose identifier contains "drill"; the production global cluster and its us-east-1 members are untouched; terragrunt reports no remaining resources under envs/dr-us-east-2; the vendor shows the recovery concluded
rollback.pass: Drill estate gone, nothing in us-east-2 still writing, and the deletion list matches exactly what this test created — no resource deleted that the test did not create
rollback.record: What was deleted and what was kept; whether a final snapshot was taken and why; anything exported before the vendor recovery was concluded

rollback.title: Prove the steady state is back — and write down what could NOT be undone
rollback.detail:
A test that leaves replication broken has negative value, so the last gate is the boring one: every mechanism green again, with evidence and a timestamp, and no orphaned us-east-2 resources quietly billing.

Then the paragraph people skip, which is the reason this step is a gate. What could this test not undo?
(a) Any write accepted in us-east-2 while it held the writer — hand reconciliation or nothing.
(b) The restored remittance copies and claim queues destroyed by concluding the vendor recovery, including anything someone was still reading out of them.
(c) Partner-side state, if containment was relaxed and something got out. A test claim that reached the clearinghouse is not yours to reverse; it is a phone call the same day.
(d) The drill cluster's data once deleted.
If the honest answer is that nothing in this run was irreversible, write "nothing" — a considered empty list is worth something; a blank field is worth nothing at all.
rollback.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier acme-adjudication-global --region us-east-1
aws s3api get-bucket-replication --bucket <claims-bucket>
aws ecr describe-registry --region us-east-1
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --region us-east-2 --query "length(SecretList)"
aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name acme-dr --region us-east-2 --max-results 5
rollback.verify: Global cluster replicating us-east-1 → us-east-2 with lag under a minute; CRR COMPLETED on objects written since teardown; ECR replication rule present and images current; replica secrets present; a backup copy completed since teardown; vendor protection resumed
rollback.pass: Every mechanism green again with evidence and a timestamp, zero orphaned us-east-2 resources, and the not-reversible list written down (or an explicit "nothing")
rollback.record: Time until each path was green; orphan check; the not-reversible list

items.notes:
Phase 1 only — DNS and live traffic are untouched, and so is the adjudication writer. That second half is new. Until 2026-09-17 step stp_a06 told the operator to fail the production Aurora global cluster over to us-east-2 inside a test whose own notes said live traffic was untouched: no fence, the lossy operation chosen over the lossless one in a planned drill, no command for the failover itself, and `terragrunt run-all destroy` as the entire rollback — a rollback that never returns the writer and, with the writer in the recovery region, causes a second and larger outage. The August run did exactly that (see dec_nopromote and the tst_aug01 record). The data gate is now three steps: measure the lag (stp_a06), restore a writable drill copy (stp_a06b), and account for every other store at T0 (stp_a06c); and the rollback leads with stp_r00, which establishes who holds the writer and returns it by graceful switchover before anything is destroyed.
Most of this estate comes back from continuous AWS-native replication plus an IaC rebuild; two components (the remittance Aurora cluster and the claim queues) come back from third-party point-in-time recovery, which is why stp_a01 and stp_a06c ask for a recovery-point age as well as a replica lag.
What this runbook still cannot prove, and nobody should claim it does: it does not measure how long a promotion takes (that is a Phase 2 game day, with the game-day wrapper and the region-switch runbook); it does not exercise the public DNS cutover, which is still manual (gap_dns1); and under containment it cannot exercise the partner clearinghouse path, whose egress-IP allowlist is a manual support ticket with days of lead time (gap_partner1). A green run here leaves both of those risks exactly where they were.
The August run died at stp_a07 (secrets); the signed-off list now exists and must be re-verified before the September run. Estimated minutes are a planning estimate, not a schedule — the gates govern advancement, never the clock.
